title: The future subjunctive
objectives: I can form the future subjunctive of regular and irregular verbs from the third person plural of the preterite.
I can use quando, assim que, logo que, depois que, enquanto and sempre que with the future subjunctive to talk about future events.
I can state real conditions with se + future subjunctive, as in Se você quiser, eu ajudo.
I can tell apart a habit or past event (indicative) from a future event (future subjunctive) in the same sentence pattern.
I can explain why the forms are spelled and stressed as they are, for example tiver, tiverem, houver and dê.

vocabulary.note: Assim means 'thus' or 'like this', and que means 'that' and joins the two clauses. Spelling: ss between vowels says s, im is a nasal i (the m only nasalizes the vowel), and in que the u is silent. The verb after it is in the future subjunctive when the event lies ahead.

example.pt: Assim que eu chegar, te ligo.
example.en: As soon as I arrive, I'll call you.
example.literal: Thus that I arrive, you I-call.

vocabulary.note: Logo also means 'soon' on its own; the conjunction is the same word plus que. Spelling: g before o is hard, as in go; qu before e says k.

example.pt: Logo que o pacote chegar, eu aviso você.
example.en: As soon as the package arrives, I'll let you know.
example.literal: Soon that the package arrives, I notify you.

vocabulary.note: Spelling: ois is the vowel o gliding into i, one beat. A word ending in is is stressed on the last syllable by default, so no accent is written.

example.pt: Depois que você terminar, podemos sair.
example.en: After you finish, we can go out.
example.literal: After that you finish, we-can leave.

vocabulary.note: With the indicative it describes a habit (sempre que chove); with the future subjunctive it describes future occasions (sempre que chover). Spelling: em before a consonant is a nasal vowel, so sempre is SEHN-pree. Avós has an acute because a word ending in o or os that is stressed on the last syllable breaks the default; the vowel is open.

example.pt: Sempre que eu puder, vou visitar meus avós.
example.en: Whenever I can, I'll visit my grandparents.
example.literal: Always that I can, I-go to-visit my grandparents.

vocabulary.note: Means 'while' for simultaneous actions and 'as long as' for an open stretch of time. It is built from en (in) and quanto (how much). Spelling: in quanto the u is pronounced (qua says kwa), unlike qu before e or i; en and an are nasal.

example.pt: Enquanto você estiver aqui, pode usar meu carro.
example.en: As long as you are here, you can use my car.
example.literal: In-how-much you are here, you-can use my car.

vocabulary.note: Said about almost any plan in everyday Brazilian speech, by religious and non-religious speakers alike; it expresses hope and humility about the future. Quiser is the future subjunctive of querer. Spelling: Deus is one syllable, DEHWS, because eu is a diphthong, with the d plain because the next vowel is not i; in quiser the qu says k and the single s between vowels says z.

example.pt: Vamos viajar em julho, se Deus quiser.
example.en: We'll travel in July, God willing.
example.literal: We-go to-travel in July, if God wants.

vocabulary.note: Stress is on the last syllable, pro-me-TER, which is the default for a word ending in r, so there is no accent.

example.pt: Prometo que te ligo assim que eu puder.
example.en: I promise I'll call you as soon as I can.
example.literal: I-promise that you I-call thus that I can.

vocabulary.note: A false friend: it looks like English 'combine' but in everyday speech means to arrange or agree on something with someone. Combinado! means 'Agreed!'. Spelling: om is a nasal o. In horário the stress is on the third to last syllable (io counts as two beats), so the acute is required; in agenda the g before e says zh.

example.pt: Vamos combinar um horário quando você souber a agenda.
example.en: Let's agree on a time when you know your schedule.
example.literal: We-go to-combine a time when you know the agenda.

vocabulary.note: Spelling: z between vowels says z, and the final o is said u, so PRAH-zoo.

example.pt: Se o prazo acabar amanhã, a gente termina hoje.
example.en: If the deadline runs out tomorrow, we'll finish today.
example.literal: If the deadline ends tomorrow, the-people finishes today.

vocabulary.note: From the verb entregar, to deliver or hand over. Spelling: en is nasal, g before a is hard, and the final a is said as a weak ah.

example.pt: A entrega será rápida se você pagar hoje.
example.en: The delivery will be quick if you pay today.

vocabulary.note: An order or parcel that has been placed and is on its way. Spelling: en and men are nasal vowels, and c before o says k.

example.pt: Quando a encomenda chegar, eu te aviso.
example.en: When the order arrives, I'll let you know.
example.literal: When the order arrives, you I-notify.

vocabulary.note: Means a budget in general and a price quote in business; pedir um orçamento is to ask for a quote. Spelling: the cedilla writes s before a, so orça is OR-sah; the stress on men is where the ending o predicts it, so no accent. Segunda is short for segunda-feira, Monday.

example.pt: Se o orçamento for aprovado, começamos na segunda.
example.en: If the quote is approved, we start on Monday.
example.literal: If the quote is approved, we-start on-the Monday.

vocabulary.note: Negócio is built from a word for 'not' and a word for leisure, so business is literally 'the absence of leisure'. Spelling: ch says sh; negócio is stressed on the third to last syllable (io counts as two beats), so it always takes an accent, the acute because the o is open; c before i says s.

example.pt: Se eles aceitarem o preço, fechamos negócio.
example.en: If they accept the price, we close the deal.
example.literal: If they accept the price, we-close business.

vocabulary.note: Spelling: an initial r says h as in English hat, and the single s between vowels says z: heh-ZEHR-va. Faço has a cedilla because ç writes s before o.

example.pt: Faço a reserva assim que você confirmar.
example.en: I'll make the reservation as soon as you confirm.
example.literal: I-make the reservation thus that you confirm.

vocabulary.note: Spelling: on is a nasal vowel, and the stress is on the last syllable by the default for r. In presença the cedilla writes s before a, and en is nasal.

example.pt: Me avise quando você confirmar a presença.
example.en: Let me know when you confirm your attendance.
example.literal: Me notify when you confirm the presence.

vocabulary.note: Re- means 'again' and marcar means to mark or to set a time, so marcar um horário is to set a time. Spelling: an initial r says h, and c before a says k.

example.pt: Se chover, vamos remarcar o passeio.
example.en: If it rains, we'll reschedule the outing.
example.literal: If it-rains, we-go to-re-mark the outing.

vocabulary.note: Previsão is pre- (before) plus visão (sight). Tempo means both time and weather, and do is de plus o. Spelling: ão is a nasal diphthong stressed on the last syllable, which is what its ending predicts, so the tilde needs no other accent; s between vowels says z.

example.pt: Se a previsão do tempo estiver certa, vai chover amanhã.
example.en: If the weather forecast is right, it will rain tomorrow.
example.literal: If the foresight of-the time is right, it-goes to-rain tomorrow.

vocabulary.note: Spelling: em is nasal. The final de is said JEE in most of Brazil, because d before the sound i says j and the unstressed final e is said i.

example.pt: Se houver tempestade, o voo vai atrasar.
example.en: If there is a storm, the flight will be delayed.
example.literal: If there-is storm, the flight goes to-delay.

vocabulary.note: Spelling: two o letters, two beats (VOH-oo). Before the 2009 spelling agreement it was written vôo; the circumflex on oo was dropped. Do not confuse it with vou, I go.

example.pt: Quando o voo sair, eu te mando uma mensagem.
example.en: When the flight leaves, I'll send you a message.
example.literal: When the flight leaves, you I-send a message.

vocabulary.note: Singular in Portuguese and used for all the luggage together: a bagagem, as bagagens. Spelling: the first g is before a and hard, the second is before e and says zh; em at the end is a nasal diphthong, which puts the stress on the second to last syllable (ba-GAH-zhayn). The h of hotel is always silent.

example.pt: Assim que a bagagem chegar, a gente vai para o hotel.
example.en: As soon as the luggage arrives, we'll go to the hotel.
example.literal: Thus that the luggage arrives, the-people goes to the hotel.

vocabulary.note: Related to rota, route. Spelling: an initial r says h, and ei is one beat: hoh-TAY-roo.

example.pt: Se tivermos tempo, vamos mudar o roteiro.
example.en: If we have time, we'll change the itinerary.
example.literal: If we-have time, we-go to-change the itinerary.

vocabulary.note: The verb is atrasar, to delay or to run late. Spelling: s between vowels says z, so a-TRAH-zoo. In houver the h is silent.

example.pt: Se houver atraso, eu aviso você.
example.en: If there is a delay, I'll let you know.
example.literal: If there-is delay, I notify you.

vocabulary.note: From aviso, a notice or warning, so avisar is to notify. Me avise is the command form from the imperative unit. Spelling: s between vowels says z, and the stress is on the last syllable by the default for r.

example.pt: Me avise quando você chegar.
example.en: Let me know when you arrive.
example.literal: Me notify when you arrive.

dialogues.title: Fechando negócio
dialogues.context: Marcos buys office equipment for his company. Patrícia, a supplier, calls to agree on delivery and payment.

lines.speaker: Patrícia
lines.pt: Bom dia, Marcos. Quando vocês quiserem receber a encomenda, é só avisar.
lines.en: Good morning, Marcos. When you want to receive the order, just let us know.
lines.literal: Good day, Marcos. When you-all want to-receive the order, it-is only to-notify.

lines.speaker: Marcos
lines.pt: Bom dia, Patrícia. Se o orçamento for aprovado, queremos a entrega até o dia vinte.
lines.en: Good morning, Patrícia. If the quote is approved, we want delivery by the twentieth.
lines.literal: Good day, Patrícia. If the quote is approved, we-want the delivery until the day twenty.

lines.speaker: Patrícia
lines.pt: Fechado. Assim que eu tiver a confirmação da fábrica, te ligo.
lines.en: Deal. As soon as I have the confirmation from the factory, I'll call you.
lines.literal: Closed. Thus that I have the confirmation of-the factory, you I-call.

lines.speaker: Marcos
lines.pt: Perfeito. Se houver algum atraso, me avise logo que você souber.
lines.en: Perfect. If there is any delay, let me know as soon as you find out.
lines.literal: Perfect. If there-is any delay, me notify soon that you know.

lines.speaker: Patrícia
lines.pt: Pode deixar. Prometo que aviso assim que eu souber de qualquer coisa.
lines.en: Will do. I promise I'll tell you as soon as I know anything.
lines.literal: Can leave. I-promise that I-notify thus that I know of any thing.

lines.speaker: Marcos
lines.pt: E o pagamento? Pago metade agora e metade depois que a encomenda chegar.
lines.en: And the payment? I'll pay half now and half after the order arrives.
lines.literal: And the payment? I-pay half now and half after that the order arrives.

lines.speaker: Patrícia
lines.pt: Pode ser. Sempre que um cliente paga assim, eu faço um desconto.
lines.en: That works. Whenever a client pays like that, I give a discount.
lines.literal: Can be. Always that a client pays thus, I make a discount.

lines.speaker: Marcos
lines.pt: Ótimo! Então, se tudo der certo, fechamos negócio hoje.
lines.en: Great! Then, if all goes well, we close the deal today.
lines.literal: Great! Then, if everything gives right, we-close business today.

lines.speaker: Patrícia
lines.pt: Combinado. Vou mandar o contrato por e-mail quando terminarmos a ligação.
lines.en: Agreed. I'll send the contract by e-mail when we finish the call.
lines.literal: Combined. I-go to-send the contract by e-mail when we-finish the call.

dialogues.title: Planejando a viagem a Gramado
dialogues.context: Isabela and Fernando plan a winter trip to Gramado and worry about the weather and the flight.

lines.speaker: Isabela
lines.pt: Fernando, vamos confirmar o roteiro? Quando a gente chegar em Porto Alegre, pegamos um carro e vamos pra Gramado.
lines.en: Fernando, shall we confirm the itinerary? When we arrive in Porto Alegre, we'll pick up a car and head to Gramado.
lines.literal: Fernando, we-go to-confirm the itinerary? When the-people arrive in Porto Alegre, we-take a car and we-go to Gramado.

lines.speaker: Fernando
lines.pt: Isso. Assim que a gente deixar a bagagem no hotel, saímos pra almoçar.
lines.en: Right. As soon as we drop the luggage at the hotel, we'll go out for lunch.
lines.literal: That. Thus that the-people leave the luggage in-the hotel, we-go-out to have-lunch.

lines.speaker: Isabela
lines.pt: Vi a previsão do tempo. Se chover muito no sábado, a gente remarca o passeio.
lines.en: I saw the weather forecast. If it rains a lot on Saturday, we'll reschedule the outing.
lines.literal: I-saw the foresight of-the time. If it-rains much in-the Saturday, the-people re-marks the outing.

lines.speaker: Fernando
lines.pt: Boa. Se houver tempestade, o voo também pode atrasar.
lines.en: Good point. If there is a storm, the flight may also be delayed.
lines.literal: Good. If there-is storm, the flight also can delay.

lines.speaker: Isabela
lines.pt: Verdade. Vou ligar pra companhia assim que eu tiver o número da reserva.
lines.en: True. I'll call the airline as soon as I have the reservation number.
lines.literal: Truth. I-go to-call to the company thus that I have the number of-the reservation.

lines.speaker: Fernando
lines.pt: Pode deixar que eu faço isso. Sempre que eu viajo, confirmo tudo com antecedência.
lines.en: Leave that to me. Whenever I travel, I confirm everything in advance.
lines.literal: Can leave that I do that. Always that I travel, I-confirm everything with antecedence.

lines.speaker: Isabela
lines.pt: Ótimo. E, se Deus quiser, vamos aproveitar o frio da serra.
lines.en: Great. And, God willing, we'll enjoy the cold of the mountains.
lines.literal: Great. And, if God wants, we-go to-enjoy the cold of-the mountain-range.

lines.speaker: Fernando
lines.pt: Se Deus quiser! Enquanto estivermos lá, só quero tomar chocolate quente.
lines.en: God willing! While we're there, all I want is to drink hot chocolate.
lines.literal: If God wants! In-how-much we-are there, only I-want to-drink chocolate hot.

dialogues.title: Antes da viagem de trabalho
dialogues.context: Gustavo is about to leave on a business trip. His friend Rafaela wants to be sure they still meet when he gets back.

lines.speaker: Gustavo
lines.pt: Rafa, vou viajar amanhã a trabalho. Quando eu voltar, a gente combina aquele jantar?
lines.en: Rafa, I'm traveling tomorrow for work. When I'm back, shall we arrange that dinner?
lines.literal: Rafa, I-go to-travel tomorrow to work. When I return, the-people combines that dinner?

lines.speaker: Rafaela
lines.pt: Combinado! Me liga assim que você chegar lá.
lines.en: Deal! Call me as soon as you get there.
lines.literal: Combined! Me calls thus that you arrive there.

lines.speaker: Gustavo
lines.pt: Prometo que ligo logo que eu puder. Se o voo atrasar, mando uma mensagem.
lines.en: I promise I'll call as soon as I can. If the flight is delayed, I'll send a message.
lines.literal: I-promise that I-call soon that I can. If the flight delays, I-send a message.

lines.speaker: Rafaela
lines.pt: Tá bom. Sempre que você viaja, esquece de avisar.
lines.en: Okay. Whenever you travel, you forget to let people know.
lines.literal: Is good. Always that you travel, you-forget of to-notify.

lines.speaker: Gustavo
lines.pt: Desta vez eu aviso, juro. E se você precisar de alguma coisa, é só falar.
lines.en: This time I'll let you know, I swear. And if you need anything, just say so.
lines.literal: Of-this time I notify, I-swear. And if you need of some thing, it-is only to-speak.

lines.speaker: Rafaela
lines.pt: Se eu precisar, falo. Depois que você voltar, quero ouvir todas as histórias.
lines.en: If I need anything, I'll say so. After you come back, I want to hear all the stories.
lines.literal: If I need, I-speak. After that you return, I-want to-hear all the stories.

lines.speaker: Gustavo
lines.pt: Pode deixar. Onde eu for, vou tirar fotos pra você.
lines.en: Will do. Wherever I go, I'll take photos for you.
lines.literal: Can leave. Where I go, I-go to-take-out photos for you.

lines.speaker: Rafaela
lines.pt: Boa viagem! Que dê tudo certo.
lines.en: Have a good trip! May everything go well.
lines.literal: Good trip! That gives everything right.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: the words and verb forms of this unit
grammar.explanation:
Nothing in this unit's spelling is new. Every word can be read and written with three ideas from the first lessons, and this note shows them at work on the words that are about to appear. First, a letter chooses its sound from its neighbours: c says k before a, o and u and s before e and i, and the cedilla ç writes s before a, o and u; g is hard before a, o and u and says zh (as in measure) before e and i; qu says k before e and i, where the u is silent, but before a the u is pronounced (quando is KWAHN-doo); a single s between two vowels says z and ss writes s; ch always and x usually say sh; an initial r, like rr, says a sound like English h; and h on its own is always silent. Second, vowels: an unstressed final e and o are said i and u, and t and d before the sound i say ch and j, final e included. A vowel followed by m or n in the same syllable is nasal, and the m or n is not a consonant sound of its own. Third, stress follows the ending: a word ending in a, e, o (with or without s) or in am, em or ens is stressed on the second to last syllable, and a word ending in anything else is stressed on the last; a written accent appears only when the stress breaks that default.

The future subjunctive forms look like infinitives, and the stress rule explains why their stress moves. Falar ends in r, so it is stressed on the last syllable: fa-LAR. Falarmos ends in os, so the stress is on the second to last: fa-LAR-mos. Falarem ends in em, so it is also stressed on the second to last, which is now the la: fa-LA-rem. The stress has moved along the word because the ending changed, and none of the three needs an accent, because each agrees with the default of its ending. The same holds for tiver, tivermos and tiverem (chee-VEHR, chee-VEHR-mos, chee-VEH-rayn), for puder, pudermos and puderem, and for every other form in the next notes. One-syllable forms such as for, vir and der carry no accent either: only stressed one-syllable words ending in a, e or o are marked.

The consonants in the verb forms follow the neighbour rule exactly. In tiver and estiver the t stands before i and says ch: chee-VEHR, is-chee-VEHR. In puder and der the d stands before a stressed e, which is not the sound i, so it stays a plain d. In disser the d stands before i and says j, and ss says s: jee-SEHR. In quiser the qu says k and the single s says z: kee-ZEHR. In fizer the z says z. In trouxer the x follows the diphthong ou and says sh. In houver the h is silent and ou is one beat: oh-VEHR. The final r of all these forms is light and varies by region, from a soft h sound in Rio to a tap or an English-style r elsewhere, and in fast speech it is often barely heard; the spelling always keeps it. Vier and vir are two words with different beats: vier is vi-ER, two beats, and vir is one beat, VEER.

Accents in the words of the unit. A word stressed on the third to last syllable always takes a mark, because no ending predicts that stress, and the vowel chooses which: negócio, férias, obrigatória and histórias have an open vowel and take the acute, while a stressed e or a before m or n in the middle of a word is written with the circumflex, as in agência and trânsito. A word ending in ia or io counts the i as its own beat, which is why all of these are stressed on the third to last. Fábrica, número, horário, sábado and ótimo follow the same third to last pattern. Até, também and já break the default of their endings, so they carry a stress mark; amanhã is stressed where its ending ã predicts, so its tilde marks the nasal sound and the stress together, as explained in the first lessons. Previsão and confirmação end in the nasal diphthong ão, whose default is the last syllable, so the tilde alone marks both the nasal sound and the stress. Você has a circumflex because it is stressed on the last syllable although its ending e predicts the second to last, and the e is closed. Avós is stressed on the last syllable although its ending os predicts the second to last, and nós is a stressed one-syllable word ending in o with s, so both need the open-vowel acute. Dê, as in Que dê tudo certo, is a stressed one-syllable word ending in e, so it must be marked, and the closed e takes the circumflex; it also keeps the verb dê apart from the unstressed small word de (of). Voo has two o letters and two beats and no accent, because the 2009 spelling agreement removed the circumflex that used to be written on it.

Three more marks appear in the examples and the tables. Saímos and saíram carry an acute on the i because of a hiatus: in sair the a and the i are two separate beats, and the mark on the stressed i keeps them from being read as one diphthong (sa-EE-mos, not SAI-mos). Será, lá and já are stressed on the last syllable although a final a predicts the second to last, so the stress-breaking acute is written. Pôr, the infinitive to put, whose future subjunctive is puser, ends in r, so the default rule needs no mark for it; its circumflex is there only to keep it apart from the small word por (by, for), as explained in the first lessons.

examples.pt: Se houver atraso, eu aviso você.

grammar.title: Forming the future subjunctive: one recipe for every verb
grammar.explanation:
Start with two terms. A clause is a group of words built around one verb. A main clause can stand on its own (eu ligo, I call). A subordinate clause depends on another clause and is introduced by a conjunction, a joining word such as quando (when) or se (if). In 'When I arrive, I'll call', 'when I arrive' is the subordinate clause and 'I'll call' is the main clause. The problem this unit solves is how to put an event that has not happened yet into a subordinate clause. English avoids the future tense there: it says 'when I arrive', not 'when I will arrive', so the plain present stands in for the future. Portuguese avoids the future tense in the same place, but it has a verb form reserved for the job, the future subjunctive.

Why not simply use the present, as English does? Because in Portuguese the present indicative in that place means something else. Quando chego, janto says that whenever I arrive, I have dinner: a routine. Learners who translate English word for word say Quando eu chego, te ligo, which careful speech reads as describing a habit (casual speech does sometimes use the present for a planned, imminent event, but the future subjunctive is the standard form). The two moods explain the split. The indicative presents an event as a fact, something that happened or regularly happens. The subjunctive presents an event as not (yet) a fact. The present subjunctive from the earlier units did this for wishes, doubts and feelings. The future subjunctive does it for events that lie ahead. It does not express doubt: Quando eu fizer trinta anos (when I turn thirty) is certain to happen and still takes it, because at the moment of speaking it has not happened. Historically the form is a survivor of a Latin tense. Spanish has almost lost it, keeping it only in proverbs and legal language, but Portuguese uses it daily.

The recipe has three steps. First, take the eles form of the preterite, which you know from the lessons on the past (falaram, comeram, partiram, and irregular ones such as fizeram and foram). Second, remove the final -am. Third, add an ending: nothing for eu, você, ele, ela and a gente; -mos for nós; -em for vocês, eles and elas. Falaram gives falar, falar, falarmos, falarem. In the regions and styles that use tu, the ending is -es: falares.

Three consequences follow. First, there are no exceptions to the recipe, unlike the present subjunctive, where a few verbs broke the eu-form rule. Every verb has a preterite, so every verb has a future subjunctive, and all irregularity is inherited from an irregular preterite (next note). Second, for a regular verb the result is spelled exactly like the infinitive, in -ar, -er and -ir verbs alike, so the eu and ele forms of comer and partir are comer and partir. No new forms have to be memorized, and the conjunction before the verb tells you which one you are looking at (a later unit meets another form which is spelled the same, which is one more reason to notice the conjunction). Third, because a regular verb keeps the letters of its infinitive, none of the spelling changes of the present subjunctive (ficar, fique; pagar, pague) occur here: chegar stays chegar, and ficar stays ficar.

grammar.title: Irregular verbs: the preterite stem carries over
grammar.explanation:
The recipe from the previous note is the same for irregular verbs, and that gives a precise rule: a verb is irregular in the future subjunctive exactly when it is irregular in the preterite. The irregular preterite stems from the lesson on the irregular past come through unchanged: tiveram gives tiver, fizeram gives fizer, puderam gives puder, quiseram gives quiser, vieram gives vier, disseram gives disser, puseram gives puser. Keep this in mind for a contrast with the present subjunctive, which started from the eu form of the present. A verb whose present is irregular but whose preterite is regular gives a regular future subjunctive: peço is irregular, but pediram is regular, so the form is pedir, not peça. The same goes for ouvir (ouviram, ouvir) and sair (saíram, sair).

Ser and ir share the preterite foram, so they share one future subjunctive, for. Se eu for professor means 'if I am a teacher' (ser) and Se eu for a São Paulo means 'if I go to São Paulo' (ir); the words after it decide which. Ver and vir form a classic trap. Ver has the preterite viram and so gives vir. Vir has the preterite vieram and so gives vier. The infinitive of vir, to come, is also spelled vir, so vir on the page may be the future subjunctive of ver or the infinitive of vir; the conjunction and the subject tell them apart. Se eu vir você means 'if I see you', and Se eu vier means 'if I come'. They differ in sound as well: vir is one beat, VEER, and vier is two, vee-EHR.

Haver is used impersonally to say that something exists, like há and the English 'there is', and the future subjunctive is houver, in the singular only: Se houver problema, me avise. In everyday speech Brazilians often use ter in the same place: Se tiver problema, me avise. Dar gives der, which produces two very common chunks: Quando der (when it is possible, literally 'when it gives') and Se tudo der certo (if everything works out, literally 'if everything gives right'). Verbs built on a base verb follow the base: manter gives mantiver, desfazer gives desfizer and prever gives previr, built the same way as ver and vir.

The forms for nós and eles are made the same way as for regular verbs, by adding -mos and -em to the eu form: tivermos and tiverem, fizermos and fizerem, formos and forem. Pay attention to the stress of these. Tiver is stressed on the last syllable, tivermos on that same syllable, and tiverem on the second to last (chee-VEH-rayn), as explained in the spelling note.

grammar.title: Time words and se: future versus habit versus past
grammar.explanation:
The same conjunction can be followed by two different moods, and the mood tells the listener which kind of time you mean. The rule is a question about the event. If it already happened, or happens as a regular fact, the verb is in the indicative. If it is still ahead, so that it is not yet a fact, the verb is in the future subjunctive. Quando cheguei is past: it happened. Quando chego is a routine: it happens regularly. Quando chegar is a future event: it has not happened. Using the wrong mood changes the meaning, so never translate the English present word for word.

The conjunctions that work this way are quando (when), assim que and logo que (as soon as), depois que (after), enquanto (while, as long as) and sempre que (whenever). Except for quando and enquanto, each of them is a time word followed by que, and the que joins the subordinate clause to the main clause. The same rule holds for all of them, which is why you learn the rule once instead of learning six constructions. Note the contrast with antes que (before), which took the present subjunctive in the earlier unit: it belongs to a group of conjunctions that always take the subjunctive whatever the time, while the time words above switch between the indicative and the future subjunctive.

The main clause, the one that carries the result, is usually in the present (Quando eu chegar, te ligo), in ir plus the infinitive (Quando eu chegar, vou te ligar), in the simple future (Quando eu chegar, ligarei) or in the imperative (Quando eu chegar, me ligue). English follows the same split: 'will' and 'going to' belong to the main clause, and the dependent clause is in the plain present. The difference is only the form of the dependent verb. Never put the future tense in the dependent clause; Portuguese, like English, does not say 'when I will arrive'.

The same logic governs real conditions with se. Use the future subjunctive after se when the condition is still open and possible: Se você quiser, eu ajudo. If the sentence states a general truth or a habit, use the indicative: Se chove, não saio (if it rains, I don't go out). A condition that is contrary to fact or purely imagined uses another tense, which the next unit covers. The clauses can come in either order, and a comma separates them when the subordinate clause is first.

grammar.title: Quem, o que, onde, como and fixed phrases
grammar.explanation:
The future subjunctive also follows question words used as relatives, that is, as words that refer to a person, thing or place inside a dependent clause: quem (who), o que (what), onde (where), como (how). When the person, thing or place is not yet identified, the identity is open, and the verb takes the future subjunctive. English builds the same idea with -ever: 'whoever', 'whatever', 'wherever', 'however'. Portuguese needs no extra ending; the mood does that job. Quem chegar primeiro escolhe (whoever arrives first chooses), Faça o que você quiser (do whatever you want), Onde você for, eu vou (wherever you go, I go), Como você preferir (however you prefer). Compare the identified case, which takes the indicative: Quem chegou primeiro escolheu (the person who arrived first chose).

The tense also sits inside several fixed expressions, which Brazilians use every day and should be learned as chunks. Three of them repeat one verb, first in the present subjunctive and then in the future subjunctive, to say 'no matter what the verb does': Seja como for (be that as it may), Custe o que custar (at any cost) and Haja o que houver (come what may). Seja is the present subjunctive of ser and haja of haver, as in the earlier unit; for and houver are the future subjunctive forms of the previous notes. The table shows the literal meaning of each next to its natural equivalent. Quando der is a very common promise which carries no fixed date, and Se bobear is colloquial and means 'if we are not careful' or, in some contexts, 'maybe'.

Quanto mais... mais... compares two changes that grow together: Quanto mais você estudar, mais vai aprender (the more you study, the more you will learn). The first part is open and future, so it takes the future subjunctive. Qualquer coisa, me avisa is the common way of saying 'if anything comes up, let me know'; qualquer coisa is 'any thing', and the sentence has no verb in the subjunctive, but it does the same job as a conditional clause.

grammar.title: Phrases in the dialogues: literal meaning and use
grammar.explanation:
Several short phrases in the dialogues work as fixed chunks. Each has a literal meaning, a natural English equivalent and a use, and the three differ, so they are set apart here.

Pode deixar is literally 'can leave' and means 'leave it to me' or 'will do'; it is the usual answer to a request. Fechado is literally 'closed' and means 'deal', the way a bargain is closed. Combinado, literally 'combined', is the past participle of combinar and means 'agreed', 'it's a deal'. É só avisar is literally 'it is only to notify', the way of saying 'just let me know'. Boa, literally 'good' in the feminine, is understood as short for a feminine phrase such as boa ideia, and means 'good point' or 'nice one'. Tá bom is literally 'is good' and means 'okay'. Pode ser is literally 'can be' and means 'that works' or 'maybe'. Dar certo is literally 'to give right' and means to work out; Que dê tudo certo is literally 'that it give everything right', a wish in the present subjunctive. Tirar fotos is literally 'to take out photos'. Boa viagem is literally 'good trip'.

Two spoken reductions appear in informal dialogue. Pra is the everyday spoken form of para, with its first vowel dropped, and tá is the spoken form of está, with its first syllable dropped. Both are normal in casual speech and in dialogue writing but less common in formal writing. A gente is literally 'the people' and is used by most Brazilians to mean 'we', with a third person singular verb: a gente combina, a gente remarca. Desta is de plus esta, so desta vez is literally 'of this time', meaning 'this time'. Rafa is a shortened form of the name Rafaela, used among friends.

culture.title: Se Deus quiser, assim que der
culture.text:
Brazilians talk about the future with a mix of optimism and caution, and the future subjunctive is at the heart of it. Se Deus quiser, literally 'if God wants', is said about almost any plan, whether or not the speaker is religious; it expresses hope and a certain humility about the unknown. Quando der, literally 'when it gives', is another everyday phrase: it means 'when it is possible' and is used both as a sincere intention and as a polite way of not committing to a date.

Making plans often takes a casual form: a gente combina, vamos marcar, qualquer coisa, me avisa. A promise like Assim que eu puder, passo aí is friendly but flexible; a firm commitment would be stated with a date and time. Fechado and combinado, literally 'closed' and 'combined', both mean 'agreed' and are the usual way of sealing an arrangement. Punctuality varies with the situation, and Brazilians usually expect a message if you are running late.

When traveling, weather and holidays shape plans. Summer brings heavy afternoon rain (chuva de verão), and the feriadão, a long weekend created by a holiday (feriado plus the ending -ão, which makes a word 'big', so 'big holiday'), fills roads and airports. Travel agents and airlines often say Caso haja alteração, avisaremos (If there is any change, we will notify you), a formal version of the same idea. Notice that caso takes the present subjunctive haja, not the future subjunctive: caso is one of the conjunctions from the earlier unit that always takes the subjunctive in its present form, while se takes the future subjunctive for an open future condition.
